structured_output.summary: For 2026, R.C. 5747.02 sets Ohio's tax at $332 plus 2.75% of taxable income above $26,050. That base accounts for the consensus's whole $332 shortfall, so the consensus ($1,589.56) is wrong. The engine has the base, the two $1,900 exemptions and the $200 retirement income credit right. However, it starts from Ohio AGI equal to federal AGI ($94,925.30) and takes no medical-care deduction under R.C. 5747.01(A)(10)(b). On the stated facts the head paid $6,500 of non-employer insurance premiums and $800 of other medical costs, totaling $7,300. Premiums count as medical care under IRC 213(d)(1)(D), and $7,300 exceeds 7.5% of federal AGI ($7,119.38), so the deduction is about $180.63. Ohio tax after the retirement credit is then about $1,916.60, roughly $5 below the reference.
structured_output.engine_step_at_issue: Determining Ohio AGI of $94,925.30. The engine applied no R.C. 5747.01(A)(10)(b) deduction for unreimbursed medical care above 7.5% of federal AGI, even though the head's $6,500 of after-tax non-employer premiums plus $800 of other medical expenses exceed that threshold.

A credit shall be allowed against a taxpayer's aggregate tax liability under section 5747.02 of the Revised Code for taxpayers who received retirement income during the taxable year and whose modified adjusted gross income for the taxable year, less applicable exemptions under section 5747.025 of the Revised Code, as shown on an individual or joint annual return is less than one hundred thousand dollars.
